source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2

coverage.syllabus: Professor Jeffrey Lubbers, Fall 2026, syllabus revised September 20, 2026

syllabusAssignments.topic: Timing and Extent of Due Process Hearings

coverage.notIncluded: 2026 supplemental immigration cases (2026 Supp. p. 1), informal-adjudication Verkuil excerpt (Canvas); to be provided separately.
coverage.status: Imported original concise study notes based solely on user's chapter 2 pages 17–76; assigned problems retained unsolved.

topics.title: § 2.1 — Welfare Termination and Mass Justice (pp. 17–29)
topics.description: Classes 5–6 · constitutional due process, Goldberg v. Kelly, welfare termination, hearing design, efficiency and mass justice.

entries.title: Fifth versus Fourteenth Amendment due process
entries.summary: The Fifth Amendment constrains federal governmental deprivations; the Fourteenth Amendment constrains state and local governmental deprivations of life, liberty, or property without due process.
entries.laymanExplanation: The government must use fair procedures before taking away a protected interest; the applicable amendment depends on which government acts.
entries.legalExplanation: Constitutional procedural due process requires governmental action affecting life, liberty, or property. Purely private acts are not subject to the Fifth or Fourteenth Amendment; state constitutions may supply additional safeguards.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 17–18
entries.elements: 1. Governmental action? 2. Protected life, liberty or property? 3. Deprivation? 4. What process is constitutionally due?
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse constitutional due process with statutory hearing rights; Chapter 3 addresses separate statutory procedures.

entries.title: Administrative deprivations that may trigger hearing rights
entries.summary: Benefits terminations, student expulsion, license revocation, land-use denials, government job or contract loss are recurring settings for administrative due process.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies make decisions affecting livelihoods, licenses, education, homes, and benefits every day.
entries.legalExplanation: These are fact patterns for identifying governmental deprivations and then determining whether a constitutionally protected entitlement or liberty interest exists.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 17–18
entries.examApplication: Identify the precise government decision and whether the person is already receiving a protected benefit or merely seeking one.

entries.title: AFDC welfare entitlement and TANF differences
entries.summary: Goldberg concerned AFDC and state general relief; Congress replaced AFDC with TANF in 1996, eliminated a federal individual entitlement and changed eligibility conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: The old welfare program in Goldberg was legally different from today's TANF system.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook warns not to assume the former AFDC entitlement model automatically describes TANF: 42 U.S.C. § 601(b) disclaims individual entitlement, while § 602(a)(1)(B)(iii) requires state administrative or appeal opportunities.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 18–19
entries.examTrap: Goldberg remains important precedent, but identify the actual statutory source of any claimed welfare entitlement.

entries.title: Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
entries.summary: Eligible welfare recipients must receive an effective pretermination evidentiary hearing; a later full hearing alone is insufficient.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: Eligible welfare recipients must receive an effective pretermination evidentiary hearing; a later full hearing alone is insufficient.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment require an evidentiary opportunity to be heard before termination of subsistence welfare benefits? Reasoning: Statutory welfare entitlements count as property; deprivation can immediately end basic subsistence. The recipient's severe private interest and government's interest in accurate decisions outweigh cost savings from immediate termination.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 19–26
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: New York cut off AFDC or general relief benefits after discussion, written notice and possible written review; only after termination was a full fair hearing available.
entries.issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment require an evidentiary opportunity to be heard before termination of subsistence welfare benefits?
entries.holding: Eligible welfare recipients must receive an effective pretermination evidentiary hearing; a later full hearing alone is insufficient.
entries.reasoning: Statutory welfare entitlements count as property; deprivation can immediately end basic subsistence. The recipient's severe private interest and government's interest in accurate decisions outweigh cost savings from immediate termination.
entries.rule: Where subsistence welfare is terminated, provide advance notice, meaningful oral presentation, confrontation and cross-examination as needed, ability to retain counsel, an impartial decisionmaker, and a decision grounded in hearing evidence with stated reasons.
entries.exam: Use to contrast with disability benefits in Mathews and to identify each necessary safeguard, especially when credibility is contested.
entries.examTrap: Goldberg does NOT require a formal judicial trial or government-appointed counsel. It requires a meaningful initial pretermination hearing.

entries.title: Goldberg's procedural ingredients
entries.summary: Before cutting off subsistence welfare: timely adequate notice; opportunity to present arguments and evidence orally; confront and cross-examine adverse witnesses; retained counsel permitted; impartial decisionmaker; decision based on the record with reasons and supporting evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: The recipient must know why benefits may stop, speak directly, challenge adverse witnesses and be heard by a neutral official.
entries.legalExplanation: A pretermination hearing may be informal without a full record or comprehensive opinion; notice must meaningfully identify the legal and factual grounds; oral presentation is vital where credibility matters.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 23–25
entries.elements: (1) Timely specific notice; (2) oral defense and evidence; (3) confrontation/cross-examination where necessary; (4) retained lawyer allowed; (5) neutral decisionmaker not responsible for the initial determination; (6) reasons and evidence supporting decision.
entries.examTrap: Seven days' notice was not held per se insufficient; whether more time is required depends on context.

entries.title: Government benefit as protected entitlement
entries.summary: Government cannot avoid due process by labeling a statutory entitlement a privilege or charity; continued qualified welfare payments may be protected property.
entries.laymanExplanation: If law gives eligible recipients a claim to payments, the government cannot simply stop them without fair process.
entries.legalExplanation: Goldberg rejects the rigid right-versus-privilege characterization and treats qualified statutory welfare benefits as protected property for procedural due process.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 20–22
entries.examApplication: Locate the statute or regulation defining eligibility and entitlement before deciding what process must occur.

entries.title: Why administrative hearings matter
entries.summary: Hearings may protect dignity, empower claimants, improve accuracy, foster acceptance, create precedent, deter careless decisions, guide discretion, aid program goals, expose systematic problems and enable judicial review.
entries.laymanExplanation: A hearing is not only about winning; it can prevent errors, make agencies accountable, and help people understand decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter presents ten possible purposes for analysis, not as a constitutionally mandated checklist.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 26–27
entries.examApplication: When discussing costs and benefits, identify error correction, dignity, consistency, administrative learning and resource burdens.

entries.title: Mass justice: Goldberg's costs and unintended consequences
entries.summary: Pretermination hearings can generate enormous caseloads and delays; critics question whether adversarial hearings help unrepresented recipients and whether internal agency reforms are preferable.
entries.laymanExplanation: More hearings can improve fairness but also consume staff resources, cause delay and make systems hard to use.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes contrast Justice Brennan's safeguards with Justice Black's concern over costly and slow adversarial proceedings, and consider Jerry Mashaw's internal administrative law approach.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 27–29
entries.examTrap: Do not mistake Justice Black's predictions or textbook discussion for the controlling Goldberg holding.

entries.title: Internal administrative law
entries.summary: Agency-created management practices and procedural safeguards adopted voluntarily, beyond externally required constitutional or statutory minimums.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency can improve how it handles cases even when courts do not force it to.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes discuss internal agency quality control as an alternative or supplement to litigation-driven procedural mandates.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 28–29
entries.examApplication: Consider internal controls for high-volume welfare, disability, and immigration adjudication.

entries.title: Justice Black's Goldberg dissent
entries.summary: Black argued that constitutionalizing costly hearings rests on subjective balancing, may delay decisions, discourage agencies from initially awarding benefits, and invades legislative policymaking.
entries.laymanExplanation: He feared that making it difficult to stop welfare payments would make agencies reluctant to start paying them.
entries.legalExplanation: The dissent challenges judicial expansion of constitutional process and forecasts escalating demands for judicial review and publicly funded counsel; it is not the majority rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 25–26
entries.examApplication: Compare dignity and subsistence with administrative cost and possible disincentives to enrollment.

topics.title: § 2.2 — Interests Protected: Liberty and Property (pp. 29–47)
topics.description: Classes 7–8 · Roth entitlement threshold, modern limits on liberty, new property, Loudermill, stigma-plus, prisoner rights and textbook problems.

entries.title: Two-stage due process analysis: protected interest first
entries.summary: Before balancing the adequacy or timing of hearings, identify a government deprivation of a protected life, liberty or property interest; if none, constitutional procedural due process does not apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: First ask whether the Constitution protects what was taken; only then ask whether the procedure was fair.
entries.legalExplanation: Roth separates existence of a protected interest from the procedural balancing test that determines the timing and content of process.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 29–31
entries.elements: Step 1: Government action + deprivation of protected liberty/property. Step 2: If triggered, determine process due under Goldberg, Mathews and context-specific precedents.
entries.examTrap: The importance or hardship of losing a benefit does not, by itself, create an entitlement under Roth.

entries.title: Board of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564 (1972)
entries.summary: No. Roth lacked a legitimate claim of entitlement to reemployment and showed no liberty impairment; due process did not require reasons or hearing.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. Roth lacked a legitimate claim of entitlement to reemployment and showed no liberty impairment; due process did not require reasons or hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does nonrenewal of a one-year nontenured public teaching appointment without reasons or hearing deprive Roth of liberty or property? Reasoning: State law and the appointment terms established no renewal entitlement, and no publicly damaging accusation or foreclosure of other employment had been shown; mere interest or desire is insufficient.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 29–34
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Roth, a nontenured professor with a one-year appointment, was not rehired; neither contract nor law promised renewal; no defamatory charges or employment disqualification were shown.
entries.issue: Does nonrenewal of a one-year nontenured public teaching appointment without reasons or hearing deprive Roth of liberty or property?
entries.holding: No. Roth lacked a legitimate claim of entitlement to reemployment and showed no liberty impairment; due process did not require reasons or hearing.
entries.reasoning: State law and the appointment terms established no renewal entitlement, and no publicly damaging accusation or foreclosure of other employment had been shown; mere interest or desire is insufficient.
entries.rule: Property requires a legitimate claim of entitlement created and defined by independent law or understanding; protected liberty interests are distinct and broader, but simple job nonrenewal is insufficient.
entries.exam: Whenever public employment or benefits are at issue, inspect statutes, contracts, regulations, policies and established understandings.
entries.examTrap: Roth did not decide his separately asserted First Amendment retaliation claim; the case was remanded.

entries.title: New property and legitimate claim of entitlement
entries.summary: Property for procedural due process includes legally protected benefits and public employment, not only traditional land or money; the claimant needs a legitimate entitlement, not a unilateral expectation.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a rule or promise gives someone a legally supported claim to keep a benefit, due process may protect it.
entries.legalExplanation: The positivist approach looks to statutes, contracts, regulations or mutually understood practices as independent sources that create the entitlement.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 33–36
entries.examApplication: Ask whether substantive criteria meaningfully constrain government discretion or instead leave award/renewal wholly discretionary.

entries.title: Liberty interests under Roth and Meyer
entries.summary: Liberty can include bodily freedom, common occupations, marriage, family, acquiring knowledge and other recognized interests, subject to later doctrinal limitations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Liberty includes more than freedom from prison, but not every government disappointment.
entries.legalExplanation: Roth quotes Meyer v. Nebraska on liberty; the chapter discusses later narrowing, including the fundamental-right approach in Muñoz and limits on reputational claims.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 31–33, 36–38
entries.examTrap: Do not equate the broad Meyer catalogue with an unlimited current procedural due process interest; address Muñoz where implicated.

entries.title: Department of State v. Muñoz, 602 U.S. 899 (2024) — notes
entries.summary: The Court rejected a due process liberty interest in bringing a noncitizen spouse to live in the United States.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: The Court rejected a due process liberty interest in bringing a noncitizen spouse to live in the United States.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does denial of a spouse's visa deprive a U.S.-citizen partner of a protected liberty interest in residing together in the United States? Reasoning: The majority applied a deeply-rooted-fundamental-right analysis and emphasized sovereign immigration admission authority, as well as indirect-injury limits; the dissent disagreed about marriage-related process.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 36–38
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: A U.S. citizen challenged a consular decision denying her noncitizen spouse a visa after the government cited an inadmissibility provision but little individualized explanation.
entries.issue: Does denial of a spouse's visa deprive a U.S.-citizen partner of a protected liberty interest in residing together in the United States?
entries.holding: The Court rejected a due process liberty interest in bringing a noncitizen spouse to live in the United States.
entries.reasoning: The majority applied a deeply-rooted-fundamental-right analysis and emphasized sovereign immigration admission authority, as well as indirect-injury limits; the dissent disagreed about marriage-related process.
entries.rule: Marriage is protected, but the majority held there is no distinct fundamental right of a U.S. citizen to reside in the United States with a noncitizen spouse.
entries.exam: Flag limits on a claimant's asserted liberty interest and distinguish direct from incidental harms.
entries.examTrap: This is a textbook note discussion, not a reproduced opinion. The chapter says the effect on older reputation cases remains uncertain.

entries.title: Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593 (1972) — notes
entries.summary: Yes. An entitlement can be grounded in mutually understood implied contract or de facto tenure, not only a written tenure provision.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: Yes. An entitlement can be grounded in mutually understood implied contract or de facto tenure, not only a written tenure provision.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Can an implied contract or institutional practice create a protected entitlement despite lack of formal tenure? Reasoning: The existing rules or understandings may support a legitimate claim to continued employment.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 38
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: A long-serving nontenured professor alleged that college guidelines and practices created an understanding that he would not be discharged absent good cause.
entries.issue: Can an implied contract or institutional practice create a protected entitlement despite lack of formal tenure?
entries.holding: Yes. An entitlement can be grounded in mutually understood implied contract or de facto tenure, not only a written tenure provision.
entries.reasoning: The existing rules or understandings may support a legitimate claim to continued employment.
entries.rule: An unwritten university practice may establish property under Roth if it genuinely creates an entitlement to continued employment.
entries.exam: Compare with Roth's express contract that ended with no renewal guarantee.

entries.title: TANF and disappearance of a federal welfare entitlement
entries.summary: TANF expressly disclaims a federal individual entitlement but requires state administrative or appeal opportunities for adversely affected recipients; state law may still create rights.
entries.laymanExplanation: Federal welfare reform changed whether federal law itself promises continued benefits.
entries.legalExplanation: The book describes unresolved issues over possible state-created entitlements despite federal TANF's no-entitlement language.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 35–36
entries.examTrap: The federal no-entitlement clause does not erase every possible state-law procedural obligation.

entries.title: State action requirement and private fair procedure
entries.summary: The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments constrain government, not ordinary private entities; certain states recognize common-law or other fair-procedure duties for powerful private institutions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A private university ordinarily isn't a government actor, but separate state-law fair process rules may still apply.
entries.legalExplanation: Falcone, Boermeester and Thomas M. Cooley are notes-based examples of nonconstitutional fair procedure; they must not be silently treated as constitutional holdings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 18, 40–41
entries.examApplication: In campus or private-association hypotheticals, determine whether the institution is public or private before identifying the legal source.

entries.title: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)
entries.summary: No. Once substantive property exists, the Constitution independently determines the required procedures; the state cannot compel the employee to take the 'bitter with the sweet.'
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. Once substantive property exists, the Constitution independently determines the required procedures; the state cannot compel the employee to take the 'bitter with the sweet.'
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Can the statute that creates a protected job entitlement also limit constitutional process to whatever procedure that statute provides? Reasoning: Legislature may define the substance of an entitlement but cannot immunize deprivation from constitutionally adequate procedures by embedding inadequate process in the statute.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 41–42
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Ohio public employees who could be fired only for cause were dismissed under state statutes allowing posttermination process but no meaningful advance hearing.
entries.issue: Can the statute that creates a protected job entitlement also limit constitutional process to whatever procedure that statute provides?
entries.holding: No. Once substantive property exists, the Constitution independently determines the required procedures; the state cannot compel the employee to take the 'bitter with the sweet.'
entries.reasoning: Legislature may define the substance of an entitlement but cannot immunize deprivation from constitutionally adequate procedures by embedding inadequate process in the statute.
entries.rule: State law may create property; federal constitutional law determines the process due to deprive a person of that property.
entries.exam: Distinguish protected interest (Roth) from timing and elements (Loudermill's short pretermination check, discussed at pp. 56–57).

entries.title: Rejecting the 'bitter with the sweet' approach
entries.summary: Procedural protections are not automatically confined to procedures written in the legislation that creates the substantive right.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government cannot give a protected entitlement and then say it can remove it without constitutionally adequate process.
entries.legalExplanation: Loudermill rejects the Arnett plurality's fusion of property and procedure; Rehnquist's dissent supports more deference to state-defined limitations.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 41–43
entries.examTrap: A statute can define the existence and scope of property but cannot conclusively define all constitutional process once that property is established.

entries.title: Job protection, licenses, standards, discretion
entries.summary: Protected property often arises from for-cause job protection, professional licenses, public education, utilities and other entitlements, but broad discretion can defeat a claim.
entries.laymanExplanation: A job label such as 'permanent' alone may not guarantee the right to keep it.
entries.legalExplanation: Bishop v. Wood is an example where state-law construction treated a supposedly permanent job as at-will; examine operative legal standards instead of labels.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 43–45
entries.examApplication: Distinguish objective conditions, good-cause limits, and entirely discretionary decisions.

entries.title: Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales, 545 U.S. 748 (2005) — notes
entries.summary: No. Police enforcement discretion prevented a protected entitlement to arrest or enforcement under these facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. Police enforcement discretion prevented a protected entitlement to arrest or enforcement under these facts.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Did the mandatory sounding restraining-order enforcement provision give the beneficiary property in police enforcement? Reasoning: The Court emphasized deeply rooted law-enforcement discretion and questioned whether an entitlement to enforcement has the characteristics of property.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 44
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: After a restraining order was violated, police declined to enforce a statutory provision stating officers 'shall arrest'; the family suffered a tragedy.
entries.issue: Did the mandatory sounding restraining-order enforcement provision give the beneficiary property in police enforcement?
entries.holding: No. Police enforcement discretion prevented a protected entitlement to arrest or enforcement under these facts.
entries.reasoning: The Court emphasized deeply rooted law-enforcement discretion and questioned whether an entitlement to enforcement has the characteristics of property.
entries.rule: Mandatory wording alone does not necessarily create an individually enforceable property entitlement when enforcement remains discretionary.
entries.exam: Analyze whether 'shall' language truly removes discretion.

entries.title: Procedure alone does not create substantive entitlement
entries.summary: Government's failure to follow a procedure required by state law does not itself establish a federal due process violation if no protected substantive interest exists.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency can violate its own procedure without necessarily violating the federal Constitution.
entries.legalExplanation: The existence of procedural rules is analytically distinct from a protected life, liberty or property interest under Roth.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 44–45
entries.examTrap: Do not treat every violation of an agency rule as a federal Due Process Clause claim.

entries.title: Stigma-plus: Paul v. Davis
entries.summary: Government-imposed reputational stigma alone ordinarily does not establish procedural due process liberty deprivation; stigma must be coupled with alteration of recognized legal status or right.
entries.laymanExplanation: Being publicly defamed by the government usually is not enough; some additional legal harm or status change is needed.
entries.legalExplanation: Paul v. Davis requires 'stigma plus'; the chapter contrasts Constantineau's additional statutory restriction on alcohol purchases and limitations in Bishop/Siegert.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 45–46
entries.elements: 1. Government publicizes stigmatizing charge; 2. additional change in legal right/status; 3. identify the process/name-clearing opportunity, if otherwise warranted.
entries.examTrap: No name-clearing hearing merely from reputational injury, and publication/termination conditions can matter.

entries.title: Paul v. Davis, 424 U.S. 693 (1976) — notes
entries.summary: No; reputational harm without a qualifying additional deprivation did not trigger procedural due process.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No; reputational harm without a qualifying additional deprivation did not trigger procedural due process.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Is defamation by police enough to constitute a liberty deprivation? Reasoning: The Court required stigma in connection with a further legal status change or right.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 45–46
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Police circulated a flyer labeling Davis an active shoplifter; no accompanying loss of legally recognized employment or status was established.
entries.issue: Is defamation by police enough to constitute a liberty deprivation?
entries.holding: No; reputational harm without a qualifying additional deprivation did not trigger procedural due process.
entries.reasoning: The Court required stigma in connection with a further legal status change or right.
entries.rule: Reputation alone is not sufficient; apply stigma-plus.
entries.exam: Use as contrast to a public employee fired with publicized dishonest-conduct allegations.

entries.title: Prison discipline: Sandin test
entries.summary: A prisoner generally has no procedural liberty entitlement for ordinary discipline, but may when a decision inevitably affects sentence length or imposes atypical and significant hardship relative to normal prison life.
entries.laymanExplanation: Routine prison discipline often is not enough; unusually severe restrictions or longer custody can be.
entries.legalExplanation: The text cites Sandin v. Conner and examples of mental hospital transfer, involuntary psychiatric medication and extreme supermax confinement.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 46
entries.elements: (1) Does the measure inevitably lengthen imprisonment? OR (2) Is the hardship atypical and significant in relation to ordinary prison life?
entries.examTrap: The mere existence of prison regulations does not by itself supply the protected liberty interest.

entries.title: Sandin v. Conner, 515 U.S. 472 (1995) — notes
entries.summary: Typically only when it inevitably lengthens confinement or imposes atypical and significant hardship compared with normal prison conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: Typically only when it inevitably lengthens confinement or imposes atypical and significant hardship compared with normal prison conditions.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: When does prison discipline invade a prisoner's protected liberty? Reasoning: The Court narrowed process claims based on routine prison disciplinary restrictions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 46
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: The Supreme Court reconsidered protected liberty claims arising from ordinary prison disciplinary segregation.
entries.issue: When does prison discipline invade a prisoner's protected liberty?
entries.holding: Typically only when it inevitably lengthens confinement or imposes atypical and significant hardship compared with normal prison conditions.
entries.reasoning: The Court narrowed process claims based on routine prison disciplinary restrictions.
entries.rule: Apply the atypical-and-significant hardship test rather than assuming any segregation creates liberty.
entries.exam: Distinguish ordinary discipline from extreme confinement or involuntary treatment.

topics.title: § 2.3 — Timing of Trial-Type Hearings (pp. 47–59)
topics.description: Classes 7–8 · Mathews balancing, emergency actions, employment termination, forfeiture and hearing delays.

entries.title: Mathews v. Eldridge three-factor balancing test
entries.summary: Once a protected interest is identified, the court weighs: (1) private interest, (2) risk of erroneous deprivation and value of added safeguards, (3) government interest including fiscal and administrative costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: To decide how much procedure is needed, weigh what the person could lose, how likely the agency is to be wrong, and what more safeguards would cost.
entries.legalExplanation: Mathews governs both timing and content of due process, using context-sensitive balancing rather than a universal demand for trial-type hearings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 48–55
entries.elements: 1. Private interest and severity/duration of deprivation. 2. Risk of error from existing procedures + probable value of alternatives. 3. Public interest, governmental function, administrative/fiscal burdens.
entries.examApplication: Write each factor separately, apply facts to each, and specify an appropriate procedure.
entries.examTrap: Do not skip Roth's protected-interest threshold or treat Mathews as a mathematical formula with numeric weights.

entries.title: Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976)
entries.summary: No. The existing advance written procedures followed by a later evidentiary hearing satisfied due process under the three-factor balance.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. The existing advance written procedures followed by a later evidentiary hearing satisfied due process under the three-factor balance.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does Fifth Amendment due process demand a live evidentiary hearing before cutting off Social Security disability benefits? Reasoning: Benefits were not means-tested subsistence welfare; medical records were comparatively reliable and written submissions useful; additional pretermination hearings would impose significant costs. The hardship from delayed appeal remained relevant.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 48–55
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: SSA terminated Eldridge's disability benefits after review of medical materials, warning, evidence disclosure and a chance to respond in writing; full ALJ hearing came after termination.
entries.issue: Does Fifth Amendment due process demand a live evidentiary hearing before cutting off Social Security disability benefits?
entries.holding: No. The existing advance written procedures followed by a later evidentiary hearing satisfied due process under the three-factor balance.
entries.reasoning: Benefits were not means-tested subsistence welfare; medical records were comparatively reliable and written submissions useful; additional pretermination hearings would impose significant costs. The hardship from delayed appeal remained relevant.
entries.rule: Timing and type of hearing are determined by weighing private injury, risk of error/value of added process and government costs.
entries.exam: Compare with Goldberg, especially the nature of fact disputes (medical documents versus disputed witness credibility) and alternative resources.
entries.examTrap: Mathews is a constitutional floor; Congress later allowed certain disability recipients to elect continuing payments pending ALJ review, as described in the notes.

entries.title: Compare Goldberg and Mathews
entries.summary: Goldberg required a pretermination oral evidentiary opportunity for subsistence welfare; Mathews permitted termination of disability payments after advance written process and later oral hearing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different benefits and types of evidence can require different procedures.
entries.legalExplanation: The need for oral testimony is greater when disputed credibility and immediate subsistence are central; disability determinations in Mathews often turned on medical records.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 47–55
entries.examApplication: Compare private hardship, reliability of written evidence and cost of immediate hearings in both cases.

entries.title: Emergency and prompt-action exception to advance hearing
entries.summary: Urgent public health or safety action may occur before a full hearing if there is an important government interest and substantial assurance that the deprivation is justified, with appropriate later process.
entries.laymanExplanation: Officials can sometimes act immediately to stop danger and provide a hearing afterward.
entries.legalExplanation: Notes discuss North American Cold Storage, FDIC v. Mallen, Hodel and Barry v. Barchi as contextual examples.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 55–56
entries.examApplication: Identify the urgency, initial evidence supporting action, and promptness/adequacy of postdeprivation review.

entries.title: Statutory change after Mathews: continuing disability benefits
entries.summary: The notes report that Congress in 1983 allowed qualifying disability recipients to elect continuation of payments pending an ALJ decision in certain cessation disputes.
entries.laymanExplanation: A statute may give more protection than the Constitution requires.
entries.legalExplanation: See the discussion of 42 U.S.C. § 423(g) and 20 C.F.R. § 404.1597a; the original Mathews constitutional holding remains distinct.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 56
entries.examTrap: Do not present a later statutory benefit-continuation option as part of the Mathews constitutional holding.

entries.title: Loudermill minimum pretermination job procedure
entries.summary: For a protected government job, before discharge the employee normally receives oral or written notice of charges, explanation of evidence and opportunity to respond, followed by a fuller posttermination hearing.
entries.laymanExplanation: An employee should get an initial chance to explain before being fired, though the first meeting need not resemble a trial.
entries.legalExplanation: The advance check asks whether reasonable grounds support the charges, not whether the employer ultimately got every fact right.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 56–57
entries.elements: Notice of charges; explanation of evidence; opportunity to present employee's side (orally or in writing); meaningful later full hearing.
entries.examTrap: Do not import all of Goldberg's cross-examination requirements into a short pretermination employment check.

entries.title: How long may a postdeprivation hearing be delayed?
entries.summary: Posttermination hearings must be sufficiently timely, but permissible delay depends on context; the notes discuss extended delays accepted in Mathews and Loudermill.
entries.laymanExplanation: A later hearing is not automatically fair if the agency postpones it indefinitely.
entries.legalExplanation: Assess length of delay, justification and resulting hardship; no universal deadline is given in this passage.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 57
entries.examApplication: Explain why delay itself may become a procedural defect.

entries.title: Summary suspension of employment and professional licenses
entries.summary: In particular urgent cases, a protected employee may be suspended without pay before a hearing when independently verifiable serious charges and government trust/safety interests support prompt action.
entries.laymanExplanation: A police officer accused of a serious crime may be removed temporarily before a hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: Gilbert v. Homar and medical/taxi licensing examples apply Mathews to brief interim deprivations with later hearing.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 57
entries.examTrap: Distinguish suspension from final termination, and note the need for meaningful later review.

entries.title: Culley v. Marshall, 601 U.S. 377 (2024) — notes
entries.summary: No separate immediate hearing was required; a timely postseizure forfeiture hearing was sufficient under the precedent discussed.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No separate immediate hearing was required; a timely postseizure forfeiture hearing was sufficient under the precedent discussed.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Must the government provide a separate immediate hearing after seizing personal property for civil forfeiture? Reasoning: The textbook says the majority relied on forfeiture precedent and history, while concurrence questioned broader forfeiture constitutionality and dissent favored earlier process.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 58
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Police seized cars in drug investigations; owners sought earlier hearings to get property back pending forfeiture proceedings.
entries.issue: Must the government provide a separate immediate hearing after seizing personal property for civil forfeiture?
entries.holding: No separate immediate hearing was required; a timely postseizure forfeiture hearing was sufficient under the precedent discussed.
entries.reasoning: The textbook says the majority relied on forfeiture precedent and history, while concurrence questioned broader forfeiture constitutionality and dissent favored earlier process.
entries.rule: For personal-property civil forfeiture, analyze the timeliness of a later forfeiture hearing rather than assuming immediate hearing is required.
entries.exam: Distinguish personal from real property and note divergent opinions.

topics.title: § 2.4 — Elements of a Hearing (pp. 59–69)
topics.description: Classes 7–8 · Ingraham, Goss, later remedies, counsel, university procedures and AI adjudication hypothetical.

entries.title: Mathews determines the elements as well as timing of hearings
entries.summary: The three-factor Mathews test determines whether the process includes oral testimony, confrontation, counsel, written submissions or later review.
entries.laymanExplanation: A meaningful hearing does not always require all the features of a courtroom trial.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter contrasts Goldberg's robust evidentiary safeguards with more limited procedures or even no prior administrative hearing in specific contexts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 59
entries.examApplication: Specify the particular missing protection and evaluate its marginal benefit under each Mathews factor.

entries.title: Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U.S. 651 (1977)
entries.summary: No. Although appreciable corporal punishment implicated liberty, historically available postdeprivation judicial remedies supplied constitutionally adequate process in that setting.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. Although appreciable corporal punishment implicated liberty, historically available postdeprivation judicial remedies supplied constitutionally adequate process in that setting.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Did the Fourteenth Amendment require pre-paddling notice and an administrative hearing? Reasoning: The majority emphasized common-law tradition, presumed low error and costs to schools; dissent argued pain cannot be undone and a brief advance conversation would help.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 59–63
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Students at a public school suffered corporal punishment, including alleged severe paddling; state tort and criminal remedies were available for excessive punishment.
entries.issue: Did the Fourteenth Amendment require pre-paddling notice and an administrative hearing?
entries.holding: No. Although appreciable corporal punishment implicated liberty, historically available postdeprivation judicial remedies supplied constitutionally adequate process in that setting.
entries.reasoning: The majority emphasized common-law tradition, presumed low error and costs to schools; dissent argued pain cannot be undone and a brief advance conversation would help.
entries.rule: Even with a protected liberty interest, a context-specific combination of substantive limits and later remedies may satisfy process without a prior administrative hearing.
entries.exam: Compare with Goss; discuss whether later damages can meaningfully prevent irreversible injury.
entries.examTrap: The Court did not hold corporal punishment implicates no liberty; it held no pre-punishment administrative hearing was required.

entries.title: Goss v. Lopez, 419 U.S. 565 (1975) — notes
entries.summary: Usually notice of charges, explanation of evidence if denied, and an opportunity for the student to tell their side, typically before exclusion absent exigency.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: Usually notice of charges, explanation of evidence if denied, and an opportunity for the student to tell their side, typically before exclusion absent exigency.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: What process is due for a school suspension of ten days or less? Reasoning: Short student suspensions implicate education property interests (and possible reputational liberty), but formal adversary procedures would be excessively burdensome.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 63–64
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Public high school students were briefly suspended for misconduct; state law guaranteed access to public education.
entries.issue: What process is due for a school suspension of ten days or less?
entries.holding: Usually notice of charges, explanation of evidence if denied, and an opportunity for the student to tell their side, typically before exclusion absent exigency.
entries.reasoning: Short student suspensions implicate education property interests (and possible reputational liberty), but formal adversary procedures would be excessively burdensome.
entries.rule: An informal give-and-take can suffice; ordinary short suspensions do not require counsel or cross-examination.
entries.exam: Use to distinguish Ingraham and disciplinary hearings from academic evaluation.

entries.title: Postdeprivation remedies and random unauthorized acts
entries.summary: When meaningful predeprivation process is impracticable, adequate later state remedies may satisfy due process for unauthorized property losses; negligence alone does not constitute a constitutional due process violation.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state need not conduct a hearing before a guard unexpectedly steals or damages property, but later remedies still matter.
entries.legalExplanation: Notes distinguish Parratt v. Taylor, Hudson v. Palmer and Daniels v. Williams; Lujan v. G & G Fire Sprinklers treats ordinary government contract disputes differently from adjudicative hearings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 64–65
entries.examTrap: Do not revive the overruled idea that simple negligence alone automatically violates procedural due process.

entries.title: Counsel in administrative hearings: retained versus appointed
entries.summary: There is generally no constitutional right to government-funded counsel in ordinary civil administrative proceedings; the right to private representation may also depend on context and statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: A person usually may hire a lawyer but cannot automatically demand that the government pay for one.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter discusses Walters (historical $10 veterans counsel-fee restriction upheld in context) and separate federal representation statute 5 U.S.C. § 500(b).
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 65–66
entries.examTrap: Do not conflate the Administrative Practice Act, 5 U.S.C. § 500(b), with the federal Administrative Procedure Act.

entries.title: Walters v. National Association of Radiation Survivors, 473 U.S. 305 (1985) — notes
entries.summary: No. Under Mathews, the former veterans-fee restriction was upheld; subsequent statutory law changed the fee system.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. Under Mathews, the former veterans-fee restriction was upheld; subsequent statutory law changed the fee system.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does due process invariably guarantee retained lawyer representation at every benefits hearing? Reasoning: The majority credited informality and the desire that veterans keep awards; the chapter contrasts Goldberg's retained-counsel statement.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 65–66
entries.sourceRole: Discussed or summarized in textbook notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Federal law once severely limited attorney fees for veterans' benefit claims; informal nonlawyer advocacy was widely available.
entries.issue: Does due process invariably guarantee retained lawyer representation at every benefits hearing?
entries.holding: No. Under Mathews, the former veterans-fee restriction was upheld; subsequent statutory law changed the fee system.
entries.reasoning: The majority credited informality and the desire that veterans keep awards; the chapter contrasts Goldberg's retained-counsel statement.
entries.rule: Counsel safeguards depend on context and governing statute; no categorical right to appointed counsel.
entries.exam: Identify the present legal provision separately from historical Walters facts.

entries.title: Academic versus disciplinary dismissals
entries.summary: Disciplinary sanctions based on contested misconduct call for more procedural safeguards than expert academic evaluations of student performance.
entries.laymanExplanation: Discipline may demand a hearing; judgments about grades or clinical ability generally receive greater deference.
entries.legalExplanation: Board of Curators v. Horowitz explains reluctance to turn academic decisions into courts, while sexual-misconduct disciplinary cases present credibility and questioning issues.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 66–67
entries.examApplication: If sexual misconduct is alleged, analyze accused's ability to test competing factual accounts, panel impartiality and public/private status.

entries.title: No relevant disputed fact, possibly no hearing
entries.summary: A hearing may add no value when the proposed dispute concerns a fact irrelevant under the governing statute; a written-only process may suffice for other decisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A hearing is pointless if proving the fact would not change the result.
entries.legalExplanation: Connecticut Department of Public Safety v. Doe held there was no entitlement to prove nondangerousness where the registry statute turned solely on conviction.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 67
entries.examApplication: Ask whether the party proposes to dispute a fact the agency legally needs to determine.

entries.title: Artificial-intelligence administrative adjudication: questions to examine
entries.summary: The assigned hypothetical proposes AI-run oral disability hearings, with ALJ review of a written record; it raises questions about credibility assessment, transparency and adequate review.
entries.laymanExplanation: A robot hearing may save money, but will claimants get a fair and understandable chance to be heard?
entries.legalExplanation: Use the Mathews framework and Chapter 2 hearing principles to identify legal questions; the problem itself remains unsolved in the problem bank.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 68
entries.examTrap: Do not treat the AI regulation proposal in the hypothetical as an actual SSA regulation.

topics.title: § 2.5 — Adjudication vs. Rulemaking (pp. 69–76)
topics.description: Classes 5–6 (syllabus lists this first) · Londoner, Bi-Metallic, general vs. particular applicability, legislative/adjudicative facts, Anaconda.

entries.title: Particular versus general applicability
entries.summary: Procedural due process normally applies to individualized adjudication depriving liberty or property, not the general adoption of legislative-style policies, even where the policies have substantial economic effects.
entries.laymanExplanation: One person's disputed tax assessment may require a hearing; a citywide tax rule ordinarily does not require a personal trial.
entries.legalExplanation: Londoner/Bi-Metallic turns principally on an individualized factual determination versus generally applicable prospective policy rather than simply the count of persons affected.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 69–74
entries.elements: 1. Is government applying a rule to specific parties based on their particular facts, or adopting broadly applicable policy? 2. Are adjudicative or legislative facts at issue? 3. If adjudication, is a protected interest deprived?
entries.examTrap: A policy can affect a small number of entities and still be rulemaking; the number alone is not dispositive.

entries.title: Londoner v. Denver, 210 U.S. 373 (1908)
entries.summary: Yes; some meaningful opportunity for argument and proof on the individualized assessment was required before the obligation became irrevocably fixed.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: Yes; some meaningful opportunity for argument and proof on the individualized assessment was required before the obligation became irrevocably fixed.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Must the affected landowner have an opportunity to be heard on a parcel-specific special assessment? Reasoning: The delegated body decided how much each particular parcel benefited and owed; written objections alone were insufficient in the circumstances.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 69–71
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: A city apportioned street-paving costs to individual parcels and accepted written objections but denied an opportunity to support objections orally before the assessments became fixed.
entries.issue: Must the affected landowner have an opportunity to be heard on a parcel-specific special assessment?
entries.holding: Yes; some meaningful opportunity for argument and proof on the individualized assessment was required before the obligation became irrevocably fixed.
entries.reasoning: The delegated body decided how much each particular parcel benefited and owed; written objections alone were insufficient in the circumstances.
entries.rule: For individualized determinations of a person's facts and assessment, meaningful hearing is constitutionally required.
entries.exam: Contrast with the general across-the-board valuation in Bi-Metallic.

entries.title: Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization, 239 U.S. 441 (1915)
entries.summary: No. General legislative-style decisions affecting all similarly situated property holders do not require individual due process hearings.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. General legislative-style decisions affecting all similarly situated property holders do not require individual due process hearings.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Must all owners receive a personal hearing before a generally applicable valuation adjustment? Reasoning: Government cannot conduct an individual town meeting with everyone affected; political representation and ordinary lawmaking channels provide structural accountability.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 71–72
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: State boards imposed a general 40% increase in taxable valuation of all Denver property, without individual oral hearings.
entries.issue: Must all owners receive a personal hearing before a generally applicable valuation adjustment?
entries.holding: No. General legislative-style decisions affecting all similarly situated property holders do not require individual due process hearings.
entries.reasoning: Government cannot conduct an individual town meeting with everyone affected; political representation and ordinary lawmaking channels provide structural accountability.
entries.rule: General applicability ordinarily removes an individual constitutional trial-type hearing requirement.
entries.exam: Contrast with Londoner's particularized benefit assessments.

entries.title: Legislative versus adjudicative facts
entries.summary: Adjudicative facts concern specific actors, events and disputed conduct; legislative facts are general facts used to make policy judgments.
entries.laymanExplanation: Who did what to whom is adjudicative; what policy generally works is legislative.
entries.legalExplanation: Particular adjudicative facts may call for oral proof or credibility testing; legislative facts may be addressed through broad information and expert study.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 73–74
entries.examApplication: Separate factual evidence about an individual violation from data supporting a policy applicable to all.

entries.title: Constitutional hearing rights versus APA notice-and-comment
entries.summary: Bi-Metallic means due process does not independently require individualized hearings for general rules, but modern administrative procedure statutes often require public notice and comment before rulemaking.
entries.laymanExplanation: No personal constitutional trial does not mean an agency can always adopt a rule in secret.
entries.legalExplanation: Constitutional rulemaking/adjudication doctrine and statutory APA rulemaking procedures have different sources and requirements.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 74
entries.examTrap: Do not claim all rulemaking is hearing-free: statutory notice-and-comment may apply.

entries.title: Anaconda Co. v. Ruckelshaus, 482 F.2d 1301 (10th Cir. 1973)
entries.summary: No. Public participation and written submission procedures satisfied statutory and due process requirements; a special trial-type adjudication was not required.
entries.laymanExplanation: In everyday terms: No. Public participation and written submission procedures satisfied statutory and due process requirements; a special trial-type adjudication was not required.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does a formally general emissions rule require a trial-type hearing because only one business is directly regulated? Reasoning: Though Anaconda was the main direct target, policy and broader community interests were involved, and protracted trial proceedings could obstruct statutory environmental goals.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 74–76
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: EPA proposed sulfur-oxide emissions restrictions framed as a rule for a Montana county where Anaconda operated the only substantial affected smelter; Anaconda demanded an adjudicatory trial.
entries.issue: Does a formally general emissions rule require a trial-type hearing because only one business is directly regulated?
entries.holding: No. Public participation and written submission procedures satisfied statutory and due process requirements; a special trial-type adjudication was not required.
entries.reasoning: Though Anaconda was the main direct target, policy and broader community interests were involved, and protracted trial proceedings could obstruct statutory environmental goals.
entries.rule: A generally applicable regulatory policy can remain rulemaking even when its immediate impact falls on one entity.
entries.exam: Distinguish Anaconda from Londoner; analyze whether the agency sets policy or resolves contested specific liability.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume a one-company practical impact automatically creates an adjudicatory hearing right.

entries.title: The single-entity regulation problem
entries.summary: A facially general rule can practically affect one regulated entity; courts assess the nature of policy judgment and affected interests, not headcount alone.
entries.laymanExplanation: A rule aimed at a single factory may still be a general policy decision.
entries.legalExplanation: Anaconda rejects an automatic trial demand; the textbook also notes scholarly criticism and the importance of legislative/adjudicative fact differences.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, pp. 74–76
entries.examApplication: For a single-factory rule, compare evidence about a future emissions standard with punishment for its past violation.

problems.title: Ten purposes of hearings and countervailing costs
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 27
problems.prompt: Evaluate whether hearings advance dignity, empowerment, acceptance, accuracy, consistency, bureaucratic accountability, discretion, program goals, agency learning and judicial review in welfare termination cases. Which rationales persuade, and what costs weigh against them?

problems.title: Justice Black's critique of Goldberg
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 28
problems.prompt: Using hearing-volume and administrative-resource information in the notes, evaluate Justice Black's prediction that Goldberg would ultimately hurt welfare recipients. Did recipients as a group gain or lose?

problems.title: Adversarial versus informal mass justice
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 28–29
problems.prompt: Would welfare recipients be better served by formal adversarial hearings, informal caseworker conferences, or internal administrative quality control? Analyze access, error correction, resources and dignity.

problems.title: Roth, Perry and discretionary public employment
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 38–39
problems.prompt: Should a nontenured public employee receive a hearing when discretionary nonrenewal is devastating to a career? Compare Roth's strict entitlement threshold with Perry's implied tenure and California's process-centered approach.

problems.title: TANF and the new-property paradox
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 35–36
problems.prompt: After federal law declared TANF not an individual entitlement, can a state structure welfare without protected property and pretermination hearings? Discuss possible state-law entitlements and unresolved issues.

problems.title: § 2.2.2 Note 9 — Doris the school tennis coach
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 46
problems.prompt: Seaside High hires part-time coaches on contracts promising renewal when work is satisfactory and the school still needs the service, with written explanation if nonrenewal is due to unsatisfactory service. Doris coaches an undefeated tennis team; the principal's daughter was benched for poor attitude. Despite needing a coach, the principal refuses renewal, gives no reason and will not discuss it. What procedural rights, if any, does Doris have under the contract and due process?

problems.title: § 2.2.2 Note 10 — Child-abuse registry
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 46–47
problems.prompt: A child welfare department places Anna on a child-abuse registry after a hotline allegation; schools and childcare employers must consult the registry before hiring, but placement can be challenged only by written submission. Anna disputes continued listing and wants work as a school counselor. Is she deprived of liberty under stigma-plus? What process is due, if any?

problems.title: Applying Mathews to errors and cost
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 55–56
problems.prompt: Should courts use independent three-factor balancing or defer to reasonable good-faith administrative choices about process? Discuss risk of error, cost, medical evidence and the role of internal administrative law.

problems.title: Emergency suspension and postdeprivation hearing
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 56–57
problems.prompt: Compare spoiled-food seizure, mine closure, bank-officer suspension and racing-license suspension: when can government act without a prior hearing, and what postdeprivation process must follow?

problems.title: § 2.3 Note 8 — Muriel's public housing eviction
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 58–59
problems.prompt: A city-owned low-income apartment complex gives Muriel and four teenage children a one-year lease allowing eviction for disturbances, with hearing only after move-out. Her sole resources are TANF and food assistance. On April 19 she receives a vague noise-violation notice requiring move-out by April 29, with a hearing on May 6 if requested; she denies wrongdoing. Should a federal court enjoin eviction pending constitutionally adequate process?

problems.title: Ingraham versus Goss: school discipline
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 63–64
problems.prompt: Compare the due process procedures owed before corporal punishment with those owed for a brief disciplinary school suspension. Why did the Court permit later tort remedies in one but require an informal conversation in the other?

problems.title: Counsel and alternative hearing formats
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 65–66
problems.prompt: When can government limit a claimant's ability to use retained legal counsel in a benefit hearing? Contrast Goldberg, Walters, the general absence of appointed civil counsel, and statutory representation rights.

problems.title: § 2.4 Note 6 — SSA disability AI hearings
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 68
problems.prompt: SSA proposes that robots powered by AI conduct initial federal disability application and termination hearings, receive oral testimony and evaluate witness credibility, with claimants able to appeal to a human ALJ who reviews only the robot's written record. As a legal services office, what objections and suggestions should be submitted in comments on this proposed regulation?

problems.title: § 2.4 Note 7 — Campus sexual violence hearing
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 68–69
problems.prompt: At Madison University, John is expelled following a disputed sexual-assault allegation. The investigator Mary also sits on the hearing panel; Jane's written statement is read but she does not attend for questioning, witnesses testify without cross-examination, and attorneys are excluded. The student contract promises no job-like security or disciplinary tenure. Evaluate John's requested safeguards, including counsel, questioning and neutrality, if Madison is (i) public or (ii) private.

problems.title: Londoner versus Bi-Metallic
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 72–73
problems.prompt: Both cases involve higher taxes. Why was individualized oral process constitutionally required for Londoner's street-paving assessment but not for Denver's general valuation increase? Apply general/particular applicability and legislative/adjudicative facts.

problems.title: § 2.5 Note 5 — Zoning ordinance and variance
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 74–75
problems.prompt: Elm City's proposed zoning ordinance broadly limits large developments, including in Ben's neighborhood. (a) At a citywide public hearing, must Ben be allowed to cross-examine the planner? (b) After enactment, if Ben seeks a shopping-center variance for 'unusual hardship,' must he receive a trial-type hearing before denial? (c) If the council proposes to grant Ben's variance, does neighbor Mary have an individual hearing right to object?

problems.title: Anaconda: a general rule affecting one company
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 2, p. 75–76
problems.prompt: Anaconda is the only major source of sulfur pollution covered by an EPA proposed countywide emissions standard. Does its singular practical exposure make the process adjudicative? What kind of facts are at issue and what process does due process require?
